extracted.intended_audience: scholars and advanced students of history of mathematics and classical number theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Pythagorean-era number-theoretic results, procedures, classifications, and worked examples (Nicomachus, Pappus, Plato, Archytas, Theon, etc.) as presented in a scholarly history/treatment of ancient arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of the several means (ten means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nicomachus and Pappus distinguish ten different 'means' (starting from arithmetic, geometric, harmonic) for three-term proportions and extend the list to ten by adding seven further means; formulae for the various means are given when a > b > c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text supplies a table of formulae (Nicomachus/Pappus numbering) showing algebraic relations that define each mean and gives examples; discussion notes differences between the two accounts and historical attributions (Eudoxus, Archytas, Hippasus, Myonides, Euphranor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic mean (one of the means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterized by the relation a + c = 2 b for three terms a > b > c (i.e. b is the arithmetic mean of a and c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example and placement: arithmetic mean is No. 1 in the table; used in musical/mathematical proportions and contrasted with geometric and harmonic means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric mean (one of the means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterized by the relation ac = b^2 for three terms a > b > c (i.e. b is the geometric mean of a and c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears as No. 2 in the list of means; used in continued geometric proportion and in Plato/Euclid contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic mean (one of the means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterized by the usual harmonic relation (equivalently 1/b = (1/2)(1/a + 1/c) or by the proportion placing b as the harmonic mean between a and c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as No. 3 in the means table; historically connected to Pythagorean musical/geometrical theories (Nicomachus, Iamblichus) and used in the 'musical' four-term proportion where two means (arithmetic and harmonic) fill a double/triple interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pappus' solutions relating means to geometric progressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pappus shows that given three terms in geometric progression a, β, γ one can form three linear functions of these to obtain sequences satisfying eight of the ten mean-relations; he supplies explicit solutions (expressions) for many of the means in terms of a, β, γ together with smallest integral examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reproduces Pappus' list of formulaic solutions (for Nicomachus/Pappus Nos. 2–6, 8–10), including smallest integer instances (e.g., a=6,b=4,c=2 for one solution) and remarks why Pappus omits linear cases (indeterminacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Platonic theorem on geometric means between squares and cubes
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's remark: between two square numbers one mean in continued geometric proportion suffices; between two cube numbers two means are necessary (i.e. number of means corresponds to plane vs solid numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent statements are proved by Euclid (Elements VIII.11, 12 for square numbers and VIII.18, 19 for plane/solid cases); Nicomachus quotes this as a 'Platonic theorem.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Archytas'/Euclid's theorem on no mean proportional for ratio (n+1):n
rubrics_metrics.description: If two numbers are in the ratio (n+1):n (i.e. the ratio n+1 to n), there exists no mean proportional between them (no geometric mean lying strictly between them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Euclid's Sectio Canonis Prop. 3; a proof by Archytas (preserved by Boethius) is essentially the same and is discussed as evidence for an early Euclidean-style Elements in Pythagorean schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of the irrationality of √2 (Pythagorean/parity proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pythagorean proof by reductio ad absurdum: assume diagonal AC and side AB are commensurable a:b in lowest terms; square relations give a^2 = 2 b^2, forcing a even, then deriving that b is also even—contradiction—hence √2 is incommensurable with 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites Aristotle's account and notes this proof is interpolated in Euclid X.117; emphasizes parity argument (odd/even contradiction) as the classical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean 'side' and 'diameter' numbers (approximants to √2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integral solutions of the Pell-type equations 2 x^2 − y^2 = ±1 give successive 'side' (x) and 'diameter' (y) numbers that provide increasingly accurate rational approximations to √2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurrence: from a solution (x,y) one can form new solutions (x+y, 2x+y) using identity (2x+y)^2 − 2(x+y)^2 = −(2x^2 − y^2) (equivalently the identity {2x + y}^2 − 2{x + y}^2 = −(2x^2 − y^2) ), and Theon of Smyrna records the generation rule and lists initial pairs (1,1),(2,3),(5,7),(12,17),.... The sum-of-squares properties and alternation of signs in the sequence are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thymaridas' 'bloom' (kirkorisma) rule for linear systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule (kirdvOrjfia / 'bloom') attributed to Thymaridas for solving a particular symmetric system of n linear equations with n unknowns of a specific form; Lamblichus states the rule algebraically and shows other systems can be reduced to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is given in words and in effect yields an explicit formula for one unknown in terms of the sum of the given constants and coefficients: (sum of certain coefficients minus S) divided by (n−2) (text shows numerator (a1 + a2 + ... + a_{n−1}) − s over denominator n−2). Lamblichus illustrates reductions and treats concrete examples (including 4-variable examples) and explains integrality conditions (use of LCM, possibly doubling L when numerator odd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of solving certain underdetermined linear systems via LCM and integrality considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: For systems like x+y = (a/(a+1))L, x+z = (b/(b+1))L, etc., where x+y+z+u = L (with L chosen as lcm of (a+1),(b+1),...), one sets L to the least common multiple and computes individual sums; if numerators cause parity/integrality issues the total L may need to be doubled to obtain integer solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives worked examples (a=2,b=3,c=4 leading to L=60 then doubled to 120; another with denominators 5,7,9 needing doubling of 315 to 630) and shows explicit computed x,y,z,u values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of rectangles whose area equals perimeter
rubrics_metrics.description: Integral solutions of xy = 2(x + y) correspond to integer rectangle sides whose area equals perimeter; solving (x−2)(y−2)=4 yields only (x,y) = (4,4) and (3,6) as integer solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by simple factorization: xy = 2(x+y) ⇔ (x−2)(y−2) = 4, and enumerating factor pairs of 4 gives the complete integral solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of numbers and sieve/GCD procedures (Nicomachus' treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nicomachus' Introductio presents classification schemes for numbers (odd/even subdivisions: evenly-even, even-odd, odd-even; odd subdivisions: prime/incomposite, secondary/composite, intermediate), definitions of perfect/deficient/abundant numbers, and elementary algorithms: Eratosthenes' sieve for primes and Euclid's algorithm for greatest common measure described verbally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book uses concrete examples rather than abstract symbolic proofs; Nicomachus illustrates sieve by striking out multiples (pass over n−1 terms to strike multiples of n) and gives the Euclidean gcd process in words. Commentary warns of pedagogical shortcomings (few rigorous proofs, induction from examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygonal numbers, gnomons, and pyramidal (solid) numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions and formation rules for triangular, square, pentagonal, ... a-gonal numbers via gnomons (triangles: successive natural numbers; squares: successive odd numbers; pentagons: arithmetic progression starting 1,4,7,... with difference 3), and formulas for a-gonal numbers and their corresponding pyramids (summation formulae and relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nicomachus shows how an a-gonal number with side n equals n + 1/2 n(n−1)(a−2) (presented without modern notation), notes relations (every square is sum of two consecutive triangular numbers), and gives formulas for pyramids (solid numbers) with an a-gonal base, including truncated pyramids and various named solid-number classes (cubes, scalene numbers, beams, tiles) together with verbal descriptions of their formation.
